events.text: Welcome to the Keegix Podcast, a weekly show about running a B and B, a cottage or a short term rental.
I'm Nicole.
Every fact we use is sourced in the description.
This is episode four.
Standards and minimums guests expect.
We'll go through Airbnb's essential amenities, the ground rules every host is measured on, smoke and carbon monoxide alarms in Canada,
what Nova Scotia asks of tourist accommodations, how to build a local guide guests actually use, and how all of this turns into the Guest Favourite badge.
My guest today is Callum.

events.text: Everything about platform rules today is as of November twenty twenty six.
Airbnb updates its help pages often, and fire rules vary by province and by town, so check the current version where you are.
Good.
Let's start with what changed this month.
As of mid November twenty twenty six, the big news for hosts is a date.

card.title: Airbnb house rules policy
card.text: Applies to all reservations booked on or after November 20, 2026

events.text: Airbnb's new house rules policy applies to every reservation booked on or after November twentieth.

card.title: Airbnb house rules policy
card.text: Applies to all reservations booked on or after November 20, 2026

events.text: And it lines up with today's topic, because it's really about standards.
Hosts can't ask for checkout tasks that take significant effort or time.
Airbnb's own examples are stripping the beds and washing the dishes.
What else is off the table?
Hosts can't set their own fines or penalties.
They can't ask guests to sign a separate contract, or ask for something like a government issued I D, unless the law requires it.
And a new rule can't be added after booking, not by message, not by a sign on the fridge, not in person.
Skift reported that hosts now choose from seven standard house rules, and that repeat violations can cost a host Superhost or Guest Favourite status.
So the practical point for today is simple.
If guests expect the place to be ready, the work of getting it ready sits with the host.
Your standards have to be built into the cleaning, not into the checkout list.
Rules vary by place, and this isn't legal advice.
Now, the essentials.
Callum, walk me through the five essentials.

events.text: So beyond the essentials, what does Airbnb actually hold hosts to?
There's a help page called the host reliability standards.
It covers accuracy, check in, cleanliness, communication and cancellations.
None of them are about luxury.
They're about the place being what you said, when you said it.
Start with accuracy.
The listing should accurately describe the home and reflect the features and amenities that will be available.
And a host shouldn't change the details of a booking after it's accepted without the guest agreeing.
So if the hot tub is broken, you tell the guest before they arrive.
You don't let them find out.

events.text: That last part matters in winter.
If the guest can't get in because the lockbox is frozen or the path isn't cleared, that's a check in failure, even if the code was right.
Cleanliness.
The place should be clean and free of health hazards before check in, and cleaned between every stay.

events.text: For messages that come in during local daytime hours, Airbnb sets response times.
If check in is more than five days away, reply within three days.
If it's close to check in, or it's time sensitive during the stay, within one hour.

events.text: One hour is a tight standard for a small host with a day job.
It is.
That's why the best small hosts answer the urgent questions before guests ask them.
Where's the key, where do I park, how does the heat work, what's the wifi.
If those answers are already in front of the guest, the one hour messages mostly stop.
And cancellations?
Short version.
Hosts should not cancel confirmed reservations, except for valid reasons outside their control.
And on ratings, there's no number published, but the page says hosts should avoid too many low ratings, and that repeated low ratings can lead to enforcement.
So the standard isn't five stars.
